title: Terence Tao: Hardest Problems in Mathematics, Physics & the Future of AI (#472)
question: In mathematics, why are flawed AI-generated proofs often harder for experts to catch than low-quality proofs written by untrained humans?
guest: We've always had human-generated mathematics that's very low quality—submissions from people who don't have the formal training and so forth. But if a human proof is bad, you can tell it's bad pretty quickly. It makes really basic mistakes. The AI-generated proofs, though, can look superficially flawless. That's partly because that's what reinforcement learning has actually trained them to do: to produce text that looks like what is correct, which for many applications is good enough. So the errors are often really subtle, and then when you finally spot them, they're really stupid—mistakes that no human would have actually made.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Flawed AI-generated proofs are harder to catch because they sever the usual link between surface polish and underlying correctness. When an untrained human writes a bad proof, the flaws tend to announce themselves: misused terminology, nonstandard notation, sloppy formatting, and obvious conceptual confusions let an expert dismiss it within minutes. Experts rely heavily on these stylistic cues as a fast filter.

Language models, by contrast, are trained to produce text that looks like professional mathematics. Their output uses correct jargon, clean LaTeX, standard proof structures, and a confident tone, so it passes every superficial check. The error is typically buried in a single subtle step: a plausible-sounding lemma that is false, a cited result that does not exist or does not say what is claimed, a case silently skipped, or a gap papered over with "it is easy to see that." Because everything around the flaw is fluent and often correct, the reviewer must verify each line carefully rather than skim, which is slow and tiring.

Mathematicians such as Terence Tao have made this point: human errors usually come with warning signs, while AI errors look flawless until checked in detail.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Mathematicians normally rely on fast heuristics to spot flawed proofs by untrained humans. Amateur manuscripts typically betray themselves immediately through surface red flags: nonstandard notation, misused definitions, naive strategies, or ignorance of standard literature. Because mastering the language and technical machinery of research mathematics historically required years of training, stylistic fluency reliably signaled baseline competence.

AI-generated proofs break this correlation by decoupling stylistic mastery from logical soundness. Trained on vast mathematical corpora, modern models produce polished LaTeX, idiomatic prose, plausible proof architectures, and relevant citations that easily pass an expert's initial "smell test." Moreover, whereas untrained humans usually make blatant conceptual errors early on, AI systems chain together locally plausible steps while burying fatal flaws deep in technical transitions—quietly omitting a hypothesis when invoking a real lemma, swapping quantifiers, overlooking a boundary case, or hiding circularity behind dense calculations. Because every passage resembles serious research, experts cannot use rapid triage and must instead verify every inference and citation line by line.

noweb.answer: Untrained humans typically betray flawed proofs through obvious surface cues—clumsy notation, informal phrasing, misunderstood definitions, or broken overarching structure—allowing mathematicians to spot trouble almost immediately using fast professional heuristics. By contrast, AI models master the exact linguistic register, formatting, and rhetorical cadence of published research. Flawed AI-generated proofs therefore mimic expert writing convincingly, organizing arguments around genuine theorems and plausible high-level strategies while burying errors inside routine-looking transitions. Rather than making glaring conceptual blunders, an AI usually commits quiet technical slips: invoking a theorem while silently omitting a necessary hypothesis, subtly swapping quantifiers, introducing disguised circularity, or bridging an invalid leap with authoritative phrases like "by standard arguments." Because mathematicians naturally treat fluency with conventions as a signal of competence and skim familiar-looking steps, this polished surface disarms their initial filters. Catching an AI’s mistake forces experts to set aside rapid pattern recognition and audit every local implication and boundary condition line by line, turning what would be an effortless rejection into slow, painstaking verification.

models.answer:
Experts rarely check every line of a proof from scratch. They rely on cues that usually go along with competence. When an untrained person writes a bad proof, it tends to show itself quickly: the notation is clumsy, terms are misused, standard results are unfamiliar, the structure is muddled, or the claims are grandiose. Those signs let a referee spot the problem fast, often within a page. Terence Tao and others have pointed out that AI-generated proofs break this link between how a proof looks and whether it's correct. Language models are very good at reproducing the style of competent mathematics, including polished LaTeX, the right jargon, confident transitions and well-organized lemmas. So a proof can read like expert work while containing a fatal gap.

AI errors are also different in kind. A human expert's mistakes usually cluster around genuinely hard steps. An AI may make an elementary false claim in the middle of an otherwise sound argument, quietly assume what it's trying to prove, cite a theorem that doesn't exist, or say "it follows easily" where nothing follows. Because these failures don't look like typical human mistakes, a reviewer's instincts don't flag them. The only reliable check is slow, line-by-line verification, or a formal proof checker like Lean.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Low-quality proofs written by untrained humans usually announce themselves immediately through nonstandard notation, muddled definitions, elementary blunders, or erratic structure, allowing mathematicians to spot fatal flaws within seconds. Flawed AI-generated proofs break those triage heuristics because they convincingly mimic the surface features of expert mathematics—polished LaTeX, idiomatic phrasing, appropriate terminology, and a plausible high-level proof strategy.

Rather than being globally incoherent, AI proofs are often locally valid for long stretches, burying a single decisive error deep inside dense, confident exposition. Common failures include quietly omitting a hypothesis of a cited theorem, glossing over a delicate edge case with phrases like "it is straightforward to verify," introducing subtle circularity, or invoking plausible-sounding but false lemmas. Because the prose reads like that of a capable colleague, experts cannot rely on fast pattern-matching and must audit every inference, boundary condition, and reference line by line—making verification far more time-consuming and error-prone.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI-generated proofs can imitate the signals mathematicians use to decide where to scrutinize an argument. They can use standard notation, choose a plausible strategy, and carry out several steps correctly, yet quietly apply a theorem without checking one of its hypotheses. The proof reads like a familiar argument, so the crucial mistake may only surface when an expert checks that step in detail.

A weak proof by a beginner often gives away where to look through inconsistent notation, a misused definition, or an abrupt leap to the conclusion. The difference is how visible the flaw is. A polished proof can make an unjustified step look routine.

models.answer: Experts can often spot a beginner’s mistake because it leaves a visible clue, such as misused notation or an unjustified leap. An AI-generated proof can use the right terminology, follow a familiar strategy, and get nearly every step right. Its flaw may be as subtle as invoking a standard theorem when one of its hypotheses has never been established. The citation looks routine, so a reader may glide past the very step that needs scrutiny. Catching the error requires checking whether the theorem actually applies, even when the surrounding argument gives little reason for suspicion.
